examples.input: the program is killed halfway through saving a changed file

results.1: the file holds either the complete old text or the complete new text, never a mix; a leftover temporary file may stay in the same folder
results.2: the file can be left cut off partway, with only part of the new text and the rest missing
results.3: no decision was made here, so what happens depends on however the file happens to be written

context.in_practice: Both routes leave a file alone if its text did not change, so its timestamp and contents stay as they were. Route 1 writes the new text to a temporary file next to the original, forces it onto the disk, gives it the original's permissions, and then swaps it into place in one step. A save is therefore all or nothing. Because the original file is replaced rather than edited, anything tied to that exact file, such as hard links or some editor and file-watcher setups, may see it as a new file. Route 2 overwrites the original file directly and keeps line endings exactly as computed. It relies on every new text being worked out and checked before anything is written, so only a disk or system error during the write can cause damage, but if that happens the file is left corrupted. Route 3 never considered the question.
context.stakes: If the program is interrupted while saving a changed file (crash, Ctrl-C, power loss, full disk), the user may end up with a file that is cut off partway through and has lost content, or with a file that is either fully old or fully new.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 costs extra code, a brief temporary file and replacing the file instead of editing it, and in return a save can never leave a half-written file; route 2 is simpler and edits the file itself, but a failure during the write can leave a file damaged; route 3 makes no deliberate choice.

plan_why: Both routes write the same bytes to the same files. They differ only in crash safety (a temp file and os.replace versus an in-place write that could be left half-written) and in how symlinked or hard-linked config files and file permissions are handled. Showing that would need a crash or OS error in the middle of a write, symlinks, hard links or non-default file modes. The sandbox can only create plain files with listed contents and show their contents, so in a normal run every implementation's output looks the same.
routes: Temp file in the same directory, fsync, copy permissions, os.replace; only changed files are touched
Write in place with newline='' only when the text changed, no temp files
